question: A student council must select a two-person welcoming committee and a three-person planning committee from among its members. There are exactly \(10\) ways to select a two-person team for the welcoming committee. It is possible for students to serve on both committees. In how many different ways can a three-person planning committee be selected?
solution:
First determine the number of council members. If there are \(n\) members, choosing a first person and then a different second person gives \(n(n-1)\) ordered selections. Each two-person team appears twice, once in each order. Thus
\[
\frac{n(n-1)}2=10,
\qquad n(n-1)=20.
\]
For integers \(n\ge2\), this product increases as \(n\) increases. Since \(5\cdot4=20\), the council has exactly five members.

Now choosing a three-person planning committee is equivalent to choosing the two members left out. Each omitted pair determines exactly one committee, and each committee determines exactly one omitted pair. There are \(10\) such pairs. Serving on the welcoming committee does not remove anyone from consideration, because membership on both committees is allowed.

There are \(10\) planning committees, choice \(\mathrm{A}\).

edges.reason: Contrasting disjoint alternatives with sequential choices helps choose an operation. An array of shirts and trousers establishes the product principle independently of the addition rule.
The criterion distinguishes combinations from permutations, requiring the ordered-selection concept for that contrast even though unordered selection can be introduced independently.

Dividing ordered counts by internal permutations supplies a standard derivation. Evaluating the supplied factorial quotient or a Pascal recurrence does not require first computing a permutation number.
C(n,k) evaluates an unordered selection count; the combination concept gives the object and its non-order-sensitive meaning.

The target uses symmetry and Pascal addition to compute/check values. Pascal recursion starting from the boundary ones can itself compute the values, so a factorial formula is not universally needed; factorial evaluation is one verification route.
